analysis.one_liner: Lets insurers charge unvaccinated people up to 50% higher premiums during the COVID-19 emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote or a single cosponsor; it sat in House subcommittees for about 14 months until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the Affordable Care Act's rules so that, during the COVID-19 public health emergency, health insurers could charge unvaccinated adults up to 50% more for their premiums. It includes guardrails: people with verified medical or religious exemptions would be spared, the extra charge could not push anyone's premium above 10% of household income, insurers would have to send 25% of the surcharge money to the Treasury, and insurers would have to promise not to raise premiums on vaccinated people. It also declares that making or using fake vaccination cards should carry serious penalties. The bill never moved after introduction.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, vaccinated enrollees would have gained the most direct protection — insurers would be barred from raising their premiums due to emergency-period costs. People who then got vaccinated would avoid the surcharge, which was the bill's central incentive. Health insurers would also gain a new source of revenue, since they would keep 75% of the extra premiums collected from unvaccinated enrollees after sending a quarter of the excess to the Treasury.

how_it_helps.text: It lets an insurer raise the premium of an unvaccinated enrollee by up to 50% of the base amount during the COVID-19 emergency period, but only if the person is vaccine-eligible, not fully vaccinated, and does not have a verified medical condition or a sincerely held religious objection.
It protects vaccinated enrollees: insurers must certify to the Department of Health and Human Services that premiums for fully vaccinated people will not go up because of emergency-period costs.

It caps the burden: the surcharge cannot push an enrollee's premium above 10% of that household's income, and before applying the increase the insurer must notify the enrollee and provide free vaccination information.
It claws back part of the insurers' new revenue: insurers must pay the Treasury 25% of the premium money collected above what they would have charged without the surcharge.

It declares that selling, buying, or presenting a counterfeit vaccination card is a serious federal crime and states that violators should face fines of at least $5,000 (sellers, the maximum penalty available under federal law).

analysis.who_pays: Unvaccinated adults without a medical or religious exemption would pay up to 50% higher premiums for as long as the COVID-19 emergency designation lasted — a charge capped at 10% of household income, meaning a family earning $40,000 could owe up to $4,000 a year extra. Insurers would keep three-quarters of that money.

drawbacks.text: The penalty falls directly on individuals: an unvaccinated enrollee could pay up to 50% more in premiums, and while the bill caps the surcharge at 10% of household income, that is still a large added cost for a low-wage family.

It hands insurers a new pricing power that the Affordable Care Act deliberately removed. Under current law, premiums in the individual and small-group markets can vary only by age, location, tobacco use, and family size — not by health status. The bill would carve vaccination status into that protected list.

Insurers would keep 75% of the surcharge revenue (the bill remits only 25% of the excess premiums to the Treasury), so the measure also creates a financial windfall for the insurance industry alongside its public-health purpose.

The bill provides no direct help with vaccine access or hesitancy; it relies on a financial penalty, which research on vaccine uptake suggests reaches some people but not those most resistant, and it leaves the medically and religiously exempt unvaccinated (as the bill itself acknowledges in its exemption conditions).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill has a real public-health logic: unvaccinated people were driving a large share of COVID hospitalizations and insurer costs, and a price signal plus premium protection for the vaccinated is one way to respond. But the design leans on a blunt financial penalty on individuals rather than on access or outreach, and it hands insurers a revenue stream the ACA had deliberately shut off, with only a 25% clawback to the Treasury. Whether the vaccination incentive would outweigh the added cost burden on low-income unvaccinated households was never tested — the bill drew no cosponsors and no committee action.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in October 2021 and referred to House committees, which sent it to subcommittees where nothing further happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ruben Gallego introduced the bill on October 19, 2021, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Judiciary Committee.
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor — the bill's cosponsor list was empty for its entire life.

Within days of introduction the bill was sent to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and a year later, on November 1, 2022, part of it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security.
No committee ever reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled on the House floor, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 with the bill dead.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained much: the bill died quietly with no cosponsors and no recorded opposition, so existing rules — including the Affordable Care Act's ban on premium variation by health status — simply stayed in place, and unvaccinated enrollees never faced the surcharge it would have allowed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; existing premium rules stayed in place

for.name: Rep. Ruben Gallego
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 19, 2021; no colleague joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on October 20, 2021 and never reported it back for a floor vote.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for over a year before referring part of it to a subcommittee in November 2022; it never received consideration.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan lineup was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would hand insurers a new power to charge unvaccinated enrollees up to 50% more during the emergency, keeping 75% of the surcharge revenue after a 25% remittance to the Treasury, while requiring them not to raise premiums on vaccinated enrollees. It carves an exception into ACA rules that currently bar premium variation by health status.

The surcharge is designed to push vaccine uptake, and the bill requires insurers to point enrollees to free vaccines, increasing demand for shots that were purchased by the federal government and administered at no cost to patients.
